# Weakness 13
> There should be a limitation section, even if it is in the appendix due to space constraints.

We add limitation in the revised version.

# Q1
> In what scenario is incorrect samples readily available other than distillation?

We appreciate the reviewer’s question. In our experiments, incorrect trajectories happen to come from a distillation pipeline, but we do not view distillation as the only or even the primary way such negatives arise in practice. Whenever a reasoning model is used in a ReAct[1] loop, incorrect samples are naturally and abundantly produced.  
Concretely, there are at least three common scenarios. 

First, RLHF and preference-learning pipelines routinely sample multiple candidate responses per prompt and ask humans to rank them; all lower-ranked or rejected candidates are effectively “incorrect” trajectories that are currently discarded or only used implicitly through pairwise preferences. 

Second, self-correction and multi-turn RL methods generate entire trajectories of failed attempts and subsequent revisions using only the model itself; these unsuccessful attempts again constitute exactly the kind of negative chain-of-thought data we study. 

Third, deployed chatbots and tutoring systems continuously log responses that users mark as wrong or revise in follow-up turns, providing large volumes of noisy but readily available incorrect samples, especially in domains with automatic checkers such as math or code.


[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629

# Q2
> Since you claim that it explores more at inference time, it will be more convincing if you could try to do some simple test-time scaling like majority voting with N samples and see if your method helps. 

We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion. We view test-time scaling with multiple samples as **orthogonal** to our main contribution, and claim that the model “explores more at inference time” is grounded in the analysis we already report under a fixed single-sample decoding protocol: the reweighted models exhibit higher entropy on the reasoning head, more diverse chain-of-thought trajectories, and, crucially, improved performance on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks compared to standard SFT, even when using the same decoding strategy as prior work. In other words, our primary goal in this paper is to show that gain-based reweighting leads to a better base policy under standard inference settings, without relying on additional test-time tricks. To keep the experimental design focused and comparable to existing SFT-based reasoning work, we therefore restrict our reported results to the single-sample setting and leave a systematic study of self-consistency and other test-time scaling strategies on top of our reweighted policy as future work.

# Q3
> Can the authors explain how 
> • We provide the first systematic study demonstrating that negative reasoning samples constitute valuable supervision 

Our claim is not that we are the first to use negative data in general, but that we are the first to systematically treat negative chain-of-thought trajectories as an independent **useful and informative** source of  supervision for reasoning SFT. Ref to line 150-152 in the revised paper.

We would like to restate our key contributions clearly. 
1. First, to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to empirically demonstrate that optimizing SFT toward negative reasoning trajectories yields consistent performance gains. 
2. Second, motivated by this finding, we propose GLOW, a simple dynamic reweighting method that improves data utilization without any manual data filtering. 

Across our experiments, GLOW improves performance under SFT and also provides a stronger initialization for subsequent RL post-training, leading to better generalization. Following your suggestions, we have added additional experiments and analyses to strengthen the evidence, and we hope they address your concerns. If anything remains unclear, we would be happy to clarify and further improve the paper.

# Weakness 11
> This can not be the right interpretation. If you MLE on any given data, the train loss will fall.
> The negative curve remains monotonic and closely tracks the positive curve, indicating that negatives provide meaningful learning signals rather than noise

We thank the reviewer for this comment.   
Our intention in the original sentence was not to claim that the shape of the loss curve alone proves the usefulness of negative trajectories. **Rather, the observation that the negative-only SFT curve remains stable and closely tracks the positive-only curve was meant as a sanity check on optimization dynamics: training on negatives does not diverge or collapse, and be haves similarly to training on positives.**   
Beyond this optimization view, the evidence that negatives are genuinely useful comes from their generalization behaviour in Tables 1 and 2. In Table 1, where we train on the math reasoning dataset, negative-only SFT consistently maintains in-domain math performance at a level comparable to positive-only SFT across all backbones (the average accuracy on Math500 / Minerva / Olympia / AMC differs only marginally between the two). At the same time, on out-of-domain benchmarks the negative-only models show clear gains: on the common-knowledge/general-reasoning benchmarks (MMLU, MMLU-Pro, BBH) the improvements are on the order of 10 percentage points on average, and on other reasoning benchmarks (ACPBench, HeadQA) the gains are around 5 points. An analogous pattern appears in Table 2 when training on the MMLU-based general reason data: negative-only SFT preserves in-domain performance on general reasoning while still improving math and other reasoning benchmarks, again indicating that negatives help generalization rather than merely being fit on the training set.

- **Difference from "negative reinforcement" in RL:** We clarified that RL-style negative reinforcement uses incorrect trajectories as *repulsive signals* under reward maximization, whereas our method stays strictly in SFT and treats negative trajectories as additional supervision examples whose weight is determined by learning dynamics $\Delta$-loss, not correctness.
- **Generality of takeaways:** We emphasized that improvements are primarily driven by the *diversity of errors* (broader trajectory coverage), rather than any single mistake category, and we clarified the intended scope/limits of this claim.

# Q1-1
We respectfully emphasize that our paper is exclusively about the SFT stage of post-training, focusing on how learning from negative reasoning trajectories reshapes the optimization landscape, improves conditioning, and **enhances cross-domain generalization** before any RL or RLVR stage is applied.  
Our work aims to answer a specific and self-contained question: *Can incorrect reasoning trajectories be leveraged as useful supervision signals during SFT, even before any RL or preference optimization is introduced?*  
This is fundamentally an SFT-level scientific question, and all our theoretical analysis, empirical setups, and ablations are designed for this setting. 

Nonetheless, during the rebuttal period we also ran small RL experiments with verl to directly verify that our approach is compatible with and beneficial to RL-style post-training . We fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B-base on GSM8K under four settings (SFT, SFT+RL, GLOW, GLOW+RL), keeping all RL-stage hyperparameters, data, and optimization details strictly identical and only varying whether the preceding SFT stage used our GLOW reweighting. Compared to the standard SFT baseline, our method yields consistent gains both before and after RL. At the SFT stage, GLOW improves MMLU from 72.24 to 73.99 (+1.75 points) and MMLU-Pro from 53.71 to 55.77 (+2.06 points), for an average gain of +1.91 points across these two OOD benchmarks. After applying the same RL procedure, GLOW+RL further improves MMLU from 72.82 to 76.47 (+3.65 points) and MMLU-Pro from 53.95 to 57.37 (+3.42 points), averaging +3.54 points. This shows that our advantage still persists after RL phase, indicating improved initialization that remains beneficial under RL-style post-training.

# Weakness 1
**Discussion of Eq. (7) and the theoretical proof**

- In Eq. (7),
  $
  L_{\text{GLOW}}^{(t)}(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^N \omega_i^{(t)}\ell_i^{(t)},
  $
  where $t$ indexes the training epoch, $\ell_i^{(t)}$ is the loss of sample $i$ at epoch $t$, $\omega_i^{(t)}$ is the cross-epoch reweighting factor for that sample, and $L_{\text{GLOW}}^{(t)}(\theta)$ is the sum of reweighted losses over all samples in epoch $t$.

- At line 404 there is a typo: the correct term is
  $
  \Delta w_i g_i g_i^\top,
  $
  not
  $
  \delta w_i g_i g_i^\top.
  $
  We apologize for the confusion. This has been corrected in the revised version.

- **Why do we introduce the subspace $U$?**  
  We are specifically interested in improving curvature along directions with small eigenvalues. The subspace $U$ is the span of these ill-conditioned directions and is a standard tool in conditioning analysis, because it isolates the “worst” part of the spectrum on which we want to show improvement.

- **Why do we introduce the energy condition?**  
  The reweighting rule naturally increases gradient energy along directions that are underrepresented, in particular those associated with small eigenvalues. The energy condition formalizes this effect and ensures that the additional mass introduced by reweighting indeed acts on the subspace $U$, so that curvature in these directions is provably enhanced.

- **Comparison with [1]**  
  Compared to [1], our work differs substantially in the reweighting signal, problem setting, and theoretical goal. [1] proposes a loss-based reweighting scheme for large-scale pretraining: it assigns weights to training examples according to their instantaneous loss and analyzes, under convex and interpolation assumptions, how this improves convergence guarantees for gradient methods and overall pretraining efficiency. In contrast, we operate in the supervised reasoning SFT stage. Our reweighting signal is not the loss itself but the loss reduction across epochs ($\Delta$ loss), which measures how much additional learning each example continues to provide. This design is motivated by our empirical finding, across multiple base models and datasets, that training on negative reasoning samples improves OOD performance, and our method is explicitly built to exploit negative reasoning trajectories to enhance OOD generalization. Conceptually, we adopt the general idea of online sample reweighting from [1], but instantiate it in a setting that is closer to practical SFT rather than generic pretraining and center it on negative examples and training dynamics. Accordingly, [1] develops global convergence results for convex objectives, whereas our theory studies improvements in conditioning and generalization for non-convex LLMs via the spectrum of the empirical Fisher and stability bounds.

The other issues regarding the formulas that you raised in Weakness 1 have been fully addressed in Appendix A.2.

[1] https://openreview.net/forum?id=gU4ZgQNsOC

# Weakness 8
> MMLU includes mathematics so it is not wholly OOD?

The point we intended to make is that the math data used for post-training and the math portions of MMLU come from substantially **different distributions**, not that there is no overlap in the broad subject category of “math.”  
Concretely, the OpenMathReasoning dataset is built from AoPS-style competition and olympiad problems with long, multi-step chain-of-thought solutions and tool-integrated reasoning traces, designed explicitly to train strong mathematical reasoning models. In contrast, MMLU math questions are short, four-choice multiple-choice items sourced from textbooks and standardized college-level exams, such as “In the complex plane, the set of points satisfying $z^2 = |z|^2$ is a (A)…(D)…”, which primarily test concise conceptual knowledge and exam-style problem solving rather than long-form solution construction.   
This mismatch in problem source (AoPS forums vs. textbooks/exams), format (open-ended CoT with long solutions vs. multiple choice), and difficulty profile (olympiad/contest vs. standard curriculum) makes the MMLU math subsets distributionally quite different from OpenMathReasoning, even though both are labeled as “math”.

# Weakness 9
> Why is some of the color coding and bolding not available for some cells in Tab. 1, 2? If it is to indicate that the cell’s result is conforming to the hypothesis, these details should be available in the Table’s caption

Thank you for the comment. We have updated the captions to explicitly describe the meaning of both formats, ensuring that the tables are now self-contained. The revised version includes the corrected captions.

# Weakness 10
> It is unclear where the empirical evidence for this is? Tab. 3 only shows the results for negative samples. If it is “richer” than positive samples we need to compare and contrast

We are delighted to further discuss this point. By “negative samples exhibit a richer variety of reasoning patterns”, we mean this in two concrete senses supported by our analysis.  
First, Table 3 quantifies error-type diversity on the negative side: following [1], we categorize each negative trajectory into 9 major error types and 22 sub-types using Gemini-2.5-Pro, and find that negative CoTs in OpenMathReasoning and MMLU are spread across a wide range of categories (calculation, completeness, logical, understanding, special cases, etc.). Positive trajectories, by construction, contain no explicit error segments to classify in the same way and are further constrained by the requirement to hit the exact ground-truth answer and a strict formatting template.   
Second, we complement this taxonomy view with a policy-entropy comparison between models trained on positives and negatives in Table 5. There, we analyze the entropy of the reasoning policy in the thinking span and answer span for $M_{pos}$ (positive-only SFT) and $M_{neg}$ (negative-only SFT). Across both math and “other” benchmarks, and under both off-policy and on-policy evaluation, $M_{neg}$ consistently shows higher entropy in the thinking span and a larger gap $\Delta H$ between thinking and answer entropy than $M_{pos}$. This indicates that negative-trained models explore a broader set of intermediate reasoning states before committing to an answer, which is consistent with their stronger cross-domain generalization. Intuitively, **a model can learn to explore a wide range of reasoning modes if such diversity is present in its training data, so the richer spectrum of negative trajectories provides a natural source for the more exploratory reasoning behaviour we observe.**

# Q4
> What about comparison or discussion with "The Surprising Effectiveness of Negative Reinforcement in LLM Reasoning"?

We thank the reviewer for pointing out this work. At a high level, both [1] and our paper highlight that “negative” reasoning samples carry important learning signal, but they do so in different parts of the post-training pipeline and under different training regimes: [1] studies negative reinforcement in an RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) setting, whereas we study negative chain-of-thought supervision in supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and how to reweight it for better generalization. 

**First, our work operates at the SFT stage, while [1] operates at the RL stage.** We focus on SFT on distilled chain-of-thought trajectories and analyze how positive-only, negative-only, and mixed SFT affect in-domain and out-of-domain generalization across math and multi-task knowledge benchmarks. In contrast, [1] decomposes RLVR updates into positive-sample reinforcement (PSR) and negative-sample reinforcement (NSR) and empirically compares these RL variants on math benchmarks.

**Second, we treat incorrect CoT trajectories as direct supervision, whereas [1] primarily uses negative samples as penalties.** Our method learns from negative trajectories themselves by feeding them into an SFT loss with gain-based reweighting, letting training decide when negatives should be upweighted or downweighted. By comparison, [1] shows that NSR-only training, which penalizes incorrect responses without explicitly reinforcing correct ones, can significantly improve Pass@k and sometimes match or surpass PPO/GRPO, but negatives there enter as a reward shaping signal rather than as supervised CoT targets.

Conceptually, the two results are complementary. [1] shows that penalizing incorrect trajectories in RL can sharpen a reasoning policy without sacrificing Pass@k diversity, while we show that training directly on negative CoT trajectories in SFT can preserve in-domain accuracy and improve out-of-domain generalization.

[1] https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.01347

# Q5
> Can the authors explain in what real-world scenario we would distill Qwen3-8B → Qwen-2.5 14B, 32B ? 

Thank you for the question. Concretely, we treat Qwen3-8B as a compact reasoning specialist that already has strong chain-of-thought capability (e.g., after expensive CoT distillation or RL on math/logic), and use it as a teacher to transfer this reasoning ability into larger, more general-purpose backbones like Qwen2.5-14B/32B that have not been explicitly trained for reasoning. In many practical systems it is prohibitively costly to re-run full reasoning-oriented training on every large backbone, so distilling the small specialist’s trajectories into larger students is a natural way to endow them with strong reasoning skills at much lower cost. This “strong reasoner → larger non-reasoner” distillation setup precisely matches the weak-to-strong reasoning (W2SR) scenario (e.g., [1]): a relatively weaker/smaller teacher is used to unlock and amplify latent reasoning ability in a stronger student, without having to directly supervise the large model with equally strong labels.

[1] https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.20072 

# Q6
> Are there any cost overheads for GLOW over the naive approach? 

Yes, GLOW does introduce a small overhead compared to the naïve SFT baseline, but it is limited to lightweight bookkeeping during training. In our implementation, GLOW keeps a dictionary that stores a few scalar statistics per training example (e.g., the current gain estimate keyed by sample ID). At each step we only perform a hash lookup and an in-place update for the samples in the current mini-batch, and then compute a scalar weight that multiplies the standard SFT loss. There are no additional forward or backward passes and no changes to the model architecture.

- **Distillation practicality (clarification):**

It is a simple, scalable, and effective way to obtain both positive and negative trajectories with consistent formatting, while emphasizing that GLOW itself depends on per-sample $\Delta$-loss dynamics rather than a hard sample-type split.

- **Overall conclusion with respect to the key concern:**
  The newly added RL table + pass@k + checkpoint analyses jointly address the reviewer’s practical-impact concerns by showing:  
  (i) **SFT gains transfer and persist under RL** (improved initialization),  
  (ii) **improvements are not an artifact of single-sample decoding** (pass@k),   
  (iii) **negatives trajectories provide stable, transferable learning signals throughout training** (checkpoint trends).

# Q1 & Q2

We thank the reviewer for raising this point and for highlighting [4]. Intuitively, one might expect that training on incorrect samples, especially in an RL-style setup where they are explicitly penalized, would bias the model toward undesirable behavior. Our experiments consistently contradict this intuition: emphasizing negative reasoning samples during SFT improves out-of-distribution (OOD) reasoning performance across many models and datasets (although slightly worse than that of positive-only training). We view this counter-intuitive effect as one of the main empirical findings of our work.

First, [4] is an RLVR-style method: the model is updated with policy gradients to maximize expected reward, and incorrect trajectories are explicitly punished through negative advantage. In contrast, GLOW remains in the SFT regime with a standard cross-entropy objective on logged trajectories. We only apply a deterministic reweighting of the loss, and the optimization target stays “match the training distribution of CoT trajectories.” As a result, negative samples in GLOW act as supervised signals within the same modeling objective, rather than as repulsive signals as in RL.

Second, after an in-depth analysis, we believe the empirical gains from negative samples are linked to their structure and diversity. Our case study in Fig. 8 shows that many negative trajectories still contain clear, well-organized reasoning steps; they are “wrong” only at the final answer, so they continue to teach task format and step-wise reasoning instead of pure noise. As shown in Fig. 1, SFT on negative samples produces slower but smoother loss curves and leads to better OOD performance than positive-only SFT, suggesting that these trajectories act as a regularizer: they prevent the model from overfitting to a narrow set of shortcut-style correct solutions. From an entropy perspective, Table 5 further shows that negative-based training preserves higher predictive entropy over candidate reasoning paths than positive-only SFT, so the model maintains a richer set of plausible solutions instead of collapsing onto a few over-confident patterns.

Overall, our results indicate that, under GLOW’s $\Delta$ loss-based reweighting within SFT, negative reasoning samples do not bias the model toward systematically incorrect answers. Instead, their structural coherence and diversity provide useful supervision that improves robustness and OOD generalization.

# Q3
IRM provides a theoretical framework for understanding why diverse environments improve generalization. We interpret “diverse erroneous reasoning patterns” as multiple environments: the model is required to perform well across these environments, which encourages it to learn more stable reasoning representations. In our setting, an environment corresponds to a distinct type of incorrect reasoning; these error types induce different distributional conditions, that is, different local data distributions from the perspective of the language model. Concretely, in our formulation, $\Phi$ denotes the hidden-state mapping that sends $(x, y_{<t})$ to $h_t$, and $w$ denotes the shared token-level classifier in the output layer. When the environments are diverse, the model must learn reasoning representations that remain stable across error patterns so that the shared head $w$ can perform reliably in all environments.

# Q4
Thank you for pointing it out. The blue and red curves come from two completely independent experiments. We sampled the same number of positive and negative samples and trained Qwen2.5-32B separately on each. The blue curve shows the loss when training only on negative samples, and the red curve shows the loss when training only on positive samples.

summary.value: This paper investigates whether incorrect reasoning samples, usually discarded in supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of LLMs, can enhance generalization. The authors show that negative samples introduce diverse reasoning patterns, slow overfitting, and increase exploration during inference, leading to significant out-of-domain (OOD) gains. They further propose GLOW, which adaptively emphasizes underexplored samples, achieving consistent improvements across tasks.

We greatly appreciate your insightful feedback on our work! We have carefully considered all comments and questions, and have revised the paper accordingly to clarify our problem setting, better position our contributions relative to prior work, and strengthen both the empirical and theoretical support for our claims. Below, we respond to each point in detail and indicate the corresponding changes in the revised version.

# Weakness 1
> As the paper mentions, the pre-training + post-training (SFT, RL) is the common paradigm. There are clear evidence that shows that RL generalizes and SFT memorizes,e.g. “SFT Memorizes, RL Generalizes: A Comparative Study of Foundation Model Post-training” Modern post-training of reasoning models never stop at SFT, but always include the RL stage as it dramatically improves performance. Given that it is possible that RL improves generalization, for this work to be practically impactful it would need to show that the generalization gains at SFT lead to improved generalization or in-distribution performance post-RL.

We appreciate the reviewer’s question regarding the practical relevance of improving SFT-stage generalization. Our motivation is not to suggest that SFT alone yields uniform gains across all tasks, but rather that the SFT stage remains a critical and highly effective component of modern LLM training. Empirically, SFT has consistently demonstrated strong sample efficiency, stable optimization behavior, and substantial improvements even without reinforcement learning. For example, [1] trains a reasoning agent using only SFT, without any RL. 

In practice, the effectiveness of downstream RL is shaped by several interacting factors: data quality, exploration dynamics, preference signal coverage, and, importantly, the model’s inherent reasoning capability before RL begins. A stronger SFT model, equipped with broader cross-domain generalization, typically explores more productively, discovers better candidate solutions, and avoids early collapse into narrow or brittle strategies. Improving the SFT foundation therefore enhances the “starting point” from which RL operates, even though quantifying this transfer precisely is outside the scope of the present study.

Our contribution should therefore be understood as strengthening this foundation: we show that negative-sample supervision and our gain-based reweighting improve the generalization behavior of SFT itself, which in turn provides a more capable substrate for any subsequent preference optimization or RL-stage refinement. Extending this line of investigation to measure downstream effects on RLHF performance is a natural and important next step, and we view it as valuable future work beyond the boundaries of this paper.

[1] https://x.com/Skywork_ai/status/1990816721251536918

# Weakness 2
>First line of the abstract is confusing. The phrasing makes it sound like SFT always uses CoT, which is incorrect. SFT with CoT is only for reasoning post-training.

We thank the reviewer for pointing out this ambiguity in the abstract. To address this, we have revised the first sentence of the abstract as follows:
> Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on chain-of-thought (CoT) trajectories is a standard component of reasoning-oriented post-training for large language models. In current practice, such CoT-based SFT typically retains only trajectories whose final answers match the ground truth, which can lead to poor generalization due to overfitting and wasted data from discarding incorrect samples.

This revision makes clear that:
1. We are discussing CoT-based reasoning SFT, not all SFT pipelines.
2. The “typically uses only correct CoT data” statement refers specifically to this reasoning post-training recipe, where rejection sampling on correctness is widely used.

# Weakness 3
>Why is there + in the data annotation in Fig. 1? This seems unnecessary as it is not increasing; it is just the performance annotation.

Thank you for raising this point. The “+X” annotations in Fig. 1 are not intended as redundant positive signs on raw performance values. Rather, they are used to explicitly mark the absolute improvement (in percentage points) achieved after SFT, so that the performance gains of positive-only and negative-only SFT can be visually distinguished more clearly. The aim is to highlight the magnitude of the improvement relative to the baseline model before SFT, not merely to restate the final accuracy.
We agree that this intention was not clearly stated in the original caption, which could make the “+” appear unnecessary. To resolve this, we have updated the caption to state that:
> Qwen2.5-14B trained with positive samples shows limited transfer beyond math, whereas models trained on negative samples generalize more broadly across reasoning tasks. \revadd{Bars report the final accuracy on each benchmark, and the “+” annotations above them denote the absolute accuracy improvement over the model before SFT.

Revised caption provided in the updated PDF; see Fig. 1 in the revised submission.

# Weakness 4
> Typo issues

We thank the reviewer for noticing these typos! We have corrected these in our revision.

# Weakness 5
> The communication is confusing. What does dominant SFT mean? Why is the idea of distillation suddenly introduced here?
> (2) Data Inefficiency: Dominant SFT relies on distilled reasoning paths and uses rejection sampling to select those leading to correct answers and formats

Thank you for pointing out this confusion.  
By “dominant SFT” we did not intend to introduce a new technical term, but to refer to the standard SFT-based reasoning post-training recipe that is widely used in current practice: starting from a pretrained LLM, one collects chain-of-thought reasoning traces from a stronger teacher model (e.g., Qwen or DeepseekV3.2) and then performs SFT on this distilled reasoning data, typically within a relatively specific reasoning domain (such as math or logic benchmarks) rather than broad multi-domain web corpora. We agree that our phrasing suggests that “Dominant SFT” is a well-defined concept, which makes the sentence harder to understand.  
Similarly, the mention of “distilled reasoning paths” in point (2) is not meant to suddenly introduce a new idea at that point, but simply to describe the data source underlying most recent reasoning SFT setups, where training trajectories are distilled from a stronger thinking model and then filtered via rejection sampling to keep only those with correct final answers and formats.
To make this clearer, we will revise the corresponding sentence as follows:
> (2) Data Inefficiency: Current reasoning post-training pipelines predominantly perform SFT on chain-of-thought trajectories distilled from a stronger teacher model, and use rejection sampling to retain only trajectories whose final answers and formats match the ground truth...

# Weakness 6
>This phrase is confusing. The communication needs revision.
While relying solely on negative samples is a possible strategy, it remains a form of rejection sampling with low data efficiency

Thank you for pointing this out. The sentence in line 89 was not intended to suggest that “negative-only SFT” is a realistic or recommended training setup. It was meant to provide a conceptual contrast that helps motivate our method. Our analysis shows that negative trajectories can contribute to generalization, but using only negatives would still amount to a rejection-sampling process, simply discarding positives instead of negatives. In that sense, both positive-only and negative-only SFT suffer from the same limitation because they filter out useful data. The core message we intended to convey is that achieving true data efficiency requires moving beyond rejection-based strategies and developing a way to make use of both correct and incorrect trajectories without discarding training signal. We have revised the text to make this intent clearer in the updated submission.

# Weakness 7
>It is not correct to call MMLU and MMLU-pro a common sense benchmark

The original MMLU paper defines them as massive multi-task evaluations of knowledge and problem-solving across 57 academic and professional subjects, and follow-up work similarly treats MMLU as a broad knowledge and reasoning benchmark rather than a dedicated commonsense dataset. In the revised version, we have replaced “common sense benchmark” with “General Reasoning benchmarks”. This change does not affect any of our experiments or conclusions.

# Weakness 2
We thank the reviewer for suggesting a comparison with [2] and [3]. At a high level, GLOW focuses on improving out-of-domain generalization for LLM reasoning during supervised fine-tuning, whereas [2] and [3] target different problems and use different reweighting criteria.
From the problem perspective, [2] studies self-improvement from self-generated data, using importance weighting to filter and reweight noisy model-generated samples so that the model can learn safely from its own outputs. [3] is a theoretical active learning work that analyzes convergence of SGD when examples are sampled based on loss or uncertainty, primarily for convex or well-behaved settings and generic classifiers. In contrast, GLOW is designed around negative chain-of-thought trajectories in LLMs and aims specifically to strengthen OOD reasoning performance during SFT, rather than to design a general data acquisition policy or a generic self-improvement filter.
From the method perspective, [2] uses an importance weight that approximates distribution shift to reweight self-generated samples, and [3] analyzes uncertainty-based sampling and proposes an adaptive step-size rule. GLOW instead reweights examples according to their loss reduction across epochs and uses this dynamic “gain” signal to decide when negative reasoning samples should be emphasized. Thus, GLOW is instantiated and validated in the context of LLM reasoning, but the underlying idea of using loss-reduction–based reweighting is in principle applicable to other supervised tasks, which we see as an interesting direction beyond the current work.

[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.09849  
[3] https://openreview.net/forum?id=GLUIuli3Sm

In summary, our work shows that negative distilled reasoning trajectories provide a strong and transferable training signal. Using these trajectories for SFT to build reasoning ability improves out-of-domain generalization under standard evaluation.

* We surprisingly find that training on negative reasoning trajectories delivers more consistent out-of-domain gains than training on positive reasoning trajectories alone.
* We analyze negative trajectories from both the data and training perspectives, and provide converging evidence from multiple diagnostic views.
* We propose GLOW, a method derived from these observations. It improves overall performance on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks. It does not require prior rejection sampling, which improves data efficiency. It also outperforms standard SFT on the full dataset.

# Weakness 1
We thank the reviewer for pointing us to [1]. In short, [1] aims to suppress negative trajectories, whereas our method aims to learn from them.  
Difference from [1] in how negative samples are used. Our work and [1] both highlight the value of incorrect trajectories, but they use them for different objectives in different ways. [1] operates in an RL setting and uses negative samples as negative reinforcement signals that reduce probability mass in those directions. In contrast, our method stays in the SFT regime: negative trajectories are treated as additional supervision, because many of them contain partially correct or diverse reasoning patterns that help improve robustness and out-of-domain generalization. GLOW reweights such samples based on learning dynamics rather than outcome correctness, providing soft, structure-aware weighting rather than RL-style repulsion. Thus, both works exploit information in incorrect trajectories, but [1] uses them as repulsive signals under a reward-maximization objective, whereas we use them as diverse training signals under a generative modeling objective.

Given our limited training resources, we were not able to include MoE architectures in this work, but we view extending GLOW to MoE models as an important direction for future work.

This is an excellent question and one we have thought about carefully. In our view, the gains do not come from a specific type of data per se, but from the diversity of errors. Compared with fully correct samples, incorrect ones expose the model to a wider range of reasoning paths. This broadens the space of trajectories the model explores during thinking, which in turn leads to better performance. Thus, the key is not one particular category of mistakes, but having many different kinds of mistakes that enrich the training signal.

# Q1
Thank you for raising this concern. In the revised PDF, we have further corrected Assumption A5. Our intended meaning is not that the conclusion is assumed to hold trivially at every training step; rather, A5 is a stylized mechanism-level assumption that captures the effect we aim to model—our reweighting upweights low-gain samples and, on average, injects curvature into under-explored directions, which then enables the subsequent conditioning/stability analysis. After the revision, the assumption more clearly emphasizes this conditional and stochastic nature (and the role of ($U_t$) as a local low-curvature subspace), making the theoretical statement explicitly a conditional guarantee about the geometry of the reweighted objective rather than a blanket claim about the entire optimization trajectory.

# Q2
Thank you for this important clarification request. Our theoretical analysis is about the **reweighted surrogate objective** that our algorithm actually optimizes:

$$
R_w^{(t)}(\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_i w_i^{(t)}\,\ell_i(\theta).
$$

We study how the induced weighting changes the geometry and stability of $R_w^{(t)}$ (e.g., Fisher/Hessian conditioning in low-curvature directions) under the stated assumptions. Importantly, while training uses dynamic reweighting, all reported performance (including OOD) is evaluated using the **standard, original evaluation protocol** on held-out benchmarks (i.e., the same metrics as vanilla ERM). Thus, our claims about **high OOD accuracy** are empirical: optimizing this reweighted ERM yields models that generalize better under the original evaluation objectives. 

# Q3
Thank you for the suggestion. We have revised Figure 3 and the corresponding text to make the definition precise. At each optimization step, we select the example with the largest upweighting signal. We then calculate, for each epoch, the fraction of negatives among these stepwise-selected examples. With this clarified definition, Figure 3 still supports the same takeaway—negatives are consistently over-represented among the most strongly upweighted examples (especially early in training), and the ratio gradually decreases as training progresses. We also agree that the weights are history-dependent; we now describe this explicitly in the text, and Figure 3 is intended to summarize the aggregate effect of this correlated reweighting dynamics.

# Q5
We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful question. In our view, GLOW and REINFORCE-style methods such as [1] address different levels of the training pipeline and are conceptually compatible rather than in conflict.
From the objective perspective, [1] is a reinforcement learning method. It updates the model by policy gradients, scales gradients by a reward (or advantage), and uses negative rewards to push probability mass away from bad trajectories. GLOW stays strictly in the supervised fine-tuning regime. We optimize a standard cross-entropy loss on logged reasoning trajectories and only reweight this loss across examples based on their loss reduction. Negative samples are not “punished”; they receive higher or lower weight depending on whether they continue to provide useful learning signal.
In STaR-style self-improvement, the verifier first selects trajectories and then uses them to form a supervised dataset. GLOW can be applied exactly at this SFT stage: once the STaR dataset is fixed, one can use Δloss-based reweighting over the selected trajectories, while any additional RL phase can still rely on reward indicators as usual. We have not explored this combination empirically, but conceptually GLOW is a supervised reweighting mechanism on CoTs, whereas [1] is a reward-driven policy optimization method, and the two are complementary rather than contradictory.

We use the cosine learning rate scheduler (lr_scheduler_type = cosine in LLaMA-Factory) and record the loss every 10 steps during training, then plot the raw, unsmoothed loss curves. We observe the same pattern across multiple datasets and base models (see Fig. 8). Based on this evidence, we hypothesize that the behavioral difference between positive and negative samples largely comes from how new examples are exposed across epochs. Positive samples are memorized more quickly and show sharper loss drops between epochs, whereas negative samples continue to produce stable loss reductions over more epochs, which is associated with better OOD generalization.

Your question touches on a very practical consideration. When compute resources are sufficient, using full chain-of-thought is generally the preferred choice for equipping LLMs with reasoning ability. For example, this is the case in methods such as STaR, as well as in the Qwen models distilled from DeepSeek-R1 released by the authors.

We appreciate the reviewer’s question. Our experiments do support the claim that “training only on negative samples can outperform training only on positive samples,” but this holds under two explicit conditions. First, the gains are observed in out-of-domain evaluation. Across multiple base models and datasets, negative-only SFT consistently achieves higher OOD performance than positive-only SFT (see Table 1 and Table 2). Second, this effect relies on the typical structure of reasoning data, where negative trajectories remain informative format and semantically diverse, and differ from positives mainly in the final answer. Under these two assumptions, our results indicate that negative-only training can indeed be more effective than positive-only training for OOD reasoning.

We are aware of this finding as well. In our setting, we do not expect this issue to arise. In RL, the problem typically comes from using vLLM for inference while training with FSDP + PyTorch/DeepSpeed. Different kernels and parallelization strategies introduce rounding errors that accumulate during autoregressive sampling, so the rollout policy μ and the policy π used to compute log π during training can diverge numerically. In SFT, by contrast, we train on pre-collected data and run both forward and backward passes within a single, consistent system, which avoids this mismatch.

> Has this work been compared with "Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking" ?

The first arXiv version of “Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking” was posted on October 1, 2025, which is **after the ICLR 2026 submission deadline** on September 24, 2025, so we could not compare against or cite it in the original submission. We will add a discussion and citation for this work in the revised version.

Conceptually, this work studies flawed chain-of-thought at the RL stage for safety alignment: RECAP is an RLHF-style method that uses counter-aligned CoT prefills and a verifiable safety reward to teach models to override unsafe reasoning and improve jailbreak robustness. In contrast, our work operates purely at the SFT stage for general reasoning, treating incorrect CoT trajectories as supervision for math and multi-task benchmarks, and proposing a gain-based reweighting scheme that improves out-of-domain generalization under standard single-sample decoding.
